problems.stem: A designer writes: "We expect the redesigned dashboard to feel more intuitive." Why is this not yet a testable usability hypothesis?
options: It does not mention the artifact by name.
"Feel more intuitive" names no observable behavior, direction, or threshold a moderated session could disconfirm.
It is too short to score as a hypothesis.
It cites a feeling, which is always invalid in design research.
problems.explanation: A testable hypothesis must predict an observable outcome with a direction and a threshold so the session can confirm or disconfirm it.

problems.stem: Which rewrite best converts the rationale "fewer fields should reduce abandonment" into a falsifiable hypothesis?
options: Learners will appreciate the cleaner onboarding flow.
The 3-field screen will be objectively better than the 7-field screen.
At least 8 of 10 first-time participants will reach the first task on the 3-field screen, versus 4 of 10 on the 7-field baseline.
Reducing fields aligns with cognitive load theory.
problems.explanation: Only this option names an observable outcome, a direction, and a threshold against a stated baseline, so it can fail.

problems.stem: You ask an AI tool to draft usability hypotheses from your design rationale. What is the defensible boundary on its output?
options: Adopt the AI hypotheses as written because they sound rigorous.
Treat each AI hypothesis as a proposal and keep only those tied to an outcome you can actually observe in your prototype session.
Reject any AI help on hypotheses because that is the designer's job.
Use AI only to make the hypotheses sound more academic.
problems.explanation: AI can propose phrasing, but the designer must verify each hypothesis names an outcome observable in the planned session.

problems.stem: A team writes: "We predict the new menu will help everyone find settings." After two sessions where 3 of 4 users found settings, they call it confirmed. What is the design-reasoning flaw?
options: Two sessions is always too few for any claim.
"Help everyone" has no failure condition, so no result could ever disconfirm it; the prediction was never falsifiable.
They should have used a survey instead of observation.
Finding settings is not a usability outcome.
problems.explanation: A hypothesis with no condition under which it could fail is unfalsifiable; any result can be read as support, which is not evidence.
